title: Scaling Laws
oneLineScope: Loss as a smooth power law in parameters, data, and compute — the empirical regularity (Kaplan et al. 2020) that made scale predictable.
prose:
By 2020 the recipe in front of the field was simple to state and expensive to follow: take the autoregressive transformer of the autoregressive-lm node, make it bigger, feed it more text, train it longer. The open question was whether that brute-force path had a knee in it — a point where returns flatten and further scale buys nothing. The surprising answer, and the subject of this node, is that over the range examined there is no such knee. The test loss falls as a clean power law in scale, straight as a ruler on log-log axes across several orders of magnitude. That single empirical fact is what turned “spend more on scale” from a gamble into a forecast.

What was measured

The quantity on the y-axis is the one you would choose: the cross-entropy loss on held-out text, in nats per token — the same negative log-likelihood the model is trained to minimize, which is exactly \(\log\) of perplexity. Kaplan et al. varied three inputs, each over a wide range, and watched the loss respond:

  • \(N\) — the number of model parameters, counting only the non-embedding weights (the attention and feed-forward matrices, not the token and position embedding tables). They found embeddings are a red herring for scaling and excluding them makes the law cleaner.
  • \(D\) — the dataset size in tokens.
  • \(C\) — the training compute, in floating-point operations, roughly \(C \approx 6 N D\): six FLOPs per parameter per token (two for the forward multiply-add, four for the backward pass). This is the back-of-envelope conversion that lets you trade parameters against tokens against a dollar budget.

The law itself

Vary one of the three while holding the others non-limiting, and the loss obeys

\[ L(N) \approx \left( \frac{N_c}{N} \right)^{\alpha_N}, \qquad L(D) \approx \left( \frac{D_c}{D} \right)^{\alpha_D}, \qquad L(C) \approx \left( \frac{C_c}{C} \right)^{\alpha_C} . \]

Here each \(\alpha\) is a positive scaling exponent — the slope of the line on log-log axes — and each subscripted constant (\(N_c, D_c, C_c\)) sets where the curve crosses \(L = 1\), the scale at which the loss would notionally reach one nat. You know this functional form cold from physics and statistics: a quantity \(y \sim x^{-\alpha}\) is a straight line of slope \(-\alpha\) once you plot \(\log y\) against \(\log x\). That is precisely what the data do. The reported exponents are small — on the order of \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\) and \(\alpha_D \approx 0.095\) for the parameter and data laws, with the compute exponent in a similar range — meaning the loss falls slowly but with metronomic regularity: each factor-of-ten in scale buys a fixed decrement in loss, again and again, with no sign of stopping inside the measured window.

It is worth saying plainly where the science is. The functional form is the finding; the exponents are fit, not derived. There is no first-principles theory here that hands you \(\alpha_N \approx 0.076\) from the architecture — these are empirical regularities of the kind you have spent a career characterizing, with confidence intervals and a domain of validity, not theorems. The remarkable content is not the particular numbers but that a relationship this simple holds this well across so many decades of scale. Treat it as you would any well-fit empirical power law: trust it firmly inside the fitted range, extrapolate beyond it only with stated caution.

One refinement keeps the form honest at the limits. A pure power law \(L \sim x^{-\alpha}\) heads to zero as the resource grows, which cannot be right — language has a nonzero entropy, so there is an irreducible floor the loss can approach but never cross. Kaplan et al. accommodate this by fitting, when both inputs are jointly varied, a combined surface that adds the two effects and tends to a positive constant rather than to zero: schematically \(L(N, D)\) behaves like an \(N\)-term plus a \(D\)-term plus that floor, so whichever of model size or data is the binding constraint dominates the loss. The clean single-variable power laws above are what you see when one factor is the bottleneck and the others are held generous; the joint fit is what tells you which knob is currently limiting you and is therefore worth turning. For a statistician this is the familiar move of writing the saturating term explicitly rather than trusting a log-linear fit out past its support.

What follows from a power law

Three consequences mattered enough to change how models were built. First, loss became predictable: fit the line on small, cheap runs and you can read off, in advance, the loss a far larger run will reach. That is what justified the capital — you were no longer betting blind on scale, you were interpolating along a measured curve. Second, performance depends strongly on the scale variables \((N, D, C)\) and only weakly on architectural shape: within reason, how you split a parameter budget between depth (number of layers \(L\)) and width (\(d_{\text{model}}\)) barely moves the loss — total \(N\) is what counts. After a decade of architecture-tinkering that result was bracing. Third, larger models are more sample-efficient: a bigger model reaches any given loss having seen fewer tokens than a smaller one would need.

That last point flips an old training instinct. The classical move is to train a model to convergence — push it until the loss stops improving on your data. Kaplan et al. argue that under a fixed compute budget this is wasteful: you do better to train a large model and stop it well short of convergence than to grind a small model all the way down. Given a compute budget \(C\), there is an optimal model size \(N\), and the leftover budget goes into tokens; pouring compute into a too-small network past the point of efficient return is the mistake the law warns against.

The correction you must carry: Chinchilla

This is the place to be careful, because the field corrected itself two years later and you should not leave with Kaplan as the last word on allocation. Kaplan's own recipe for spending a compute budget leaned heavily toward model size: their analysis suggested that as you scale compute, most of it should go into more parameters and comparatively little into more data. Acting on that, the large models of 2020–2021 were built very big and trained on relatively few tokens.

In 2022 Hoffmann et al. — the Chinchilla paper — redid the compute-optimal analysis more carefully and reached a sharply different allocation: for compute-optimal training, model size and the number of training tokens should scale in roughly equal proportion, about \(1\!:\!1\), as the budget grows. By that accounting the headline models that preceded it were significantly under-trained — too many parameters chasing too little data. Their demonstration was a model (Chinchilla) substantially smaller than a contemporary giant but trained on far more tokens, which nonetheless outperformed it across the board at equal compute. The clean way to hold both papers in mind: Kaplan established that loss is a power law in scale — the foundational, still-standing result — and Chinchilla corrected the recipe for how to divide a fixed budget between \(N\) and \(D\). The straight lines were right; the early advice on which line to walk along was not.

Where it connects

This node sits downstream of the data-and-compute story — the corpora and hardware that supplied the \(D\) and \(C\) the laws are written in — and of autoregressive-lm, whose cross-entropy objective is the very loss being measured. It leads directly to in-context-learning: once you believe loss falls predictably with scale, the rational move is to build the largest model the curve and the budget allow, and it was exactly such a model, GPT-3, whose ability to learn a task from examples in its prompt — without any weight update — became the next surprise. Scaling laws are the economic argument that made that model worth building.

diagrams.caption: The iconic scaling-law plot: test loss falls as a straight line against compute (and against model size N and dataset size D) on log-log axes; the slope is the power-law exponent.
diagrams.altText: Three small log-log plots side by side. In each, the horizontal axis is log scale and the vertical axis is the test cross-entropy loss on a log scale. The left plot has loss versus training compute C; the middle plot has loss versus model parameters N; the right plot has loss versus dataset size D. In every plot the data form a descending straight line spanning several orders of magnitude, and the line's slope is labeled as the negative power-law exponent (minus alpha). A note reads: straight line on log-log axes means loss is a power law in that quantity.

Each plot has a horizontal axis labeled as a logarithmic scale and a vertical axis labeled 'test loss L (log scale)'. Left plot: horizontal axis 'training compute C (FLOPs, log)'. Middle plot: horizontal axis 'model size N (params, log)'. Right plot: horizontal axis 'dataset size D (tokens, log)'. In each plot draw a single descending straight line of data points running from upper-left to lower-right, spanning the full width to suggest several orders of magnitude. Label the slope of each line with its exponent: the compute plot 'slope = −alpha_C', the size plot 'slope = −alpha_N', the data plot 'slope = −alpha_D'. Emphasize the straightness of the lines as the central message. Add one margin note with a leader line pointing at a line: 'straight on log-log axes = power law: L is proportional to x to the minus alpha'. Structural diagram: the axes (both log), the descending straight lines, and the slope-equals-exponent labels must be exact. Do not put specific numeric loss values on the axes.

diagrams.caption: More parameters plus more data plus more compute drive the loss down predictably along the curve — with Chinchilla's later correction that model size and tokens should scale together.
diagrams.altText: On the left, three stacked inputs labeled more parameters N, more data D, and more compute C feed into a downhill arrow. The arrow leads to a lower, predictable loss on the right, drawn as a ball rolling down a smooth slope. A separate note at the bottom reads: Chinchilla 2022 correction — for a fixed compute budget, scale model size N and training tokens D together, roughly one to one; earlier large models were under-trained on data.

Reinforce the 'predictable' idea by drawing the descent as a smooth downward slope with a ball partway down it, suggesting you can see where it is heading. Earlier large models had too many parameters for too little data (under-trained).' Emphasize the contrast between the main message (scale everything up, loss goes down predictably) and the correction (balance N against D). No equations beyond the simple ratio 1:1; no axes or plots — this is the intuition companion to the log-log plot. Conceptual analogy: vibe over precise labels.

bibliography.citation: Kaplan, J., McCandlish, S., et al. (2020). "Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models." arXiv:2001.08361.
bibliography.annotation: The foundational result. §1 (Summary) states the power laws and exponents; §3 fits L(N), L(D), L(C); §6 makes the compute-optimal / sample-efficiency / 'don't train small models to convergence' argument. Note its allocation recipe was later revised by Chinchilla — read §6 with that in mind. The C ≈ 6ND estimate is in the appendix.

bibliography.citation: Hoffmann, J., Borgeaud, S., et al. (2022). "Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models" (Chinchilla). arXiv:2203.15556.
bibliography.annotation: The crucial correction to Kaplan's allocation. §3 derives, by three methods, that model size and training tokens should scale roughly equally (≈1:1) for compute-optimal training, implying prior large models were under-trained on data. Read it as the revised recipe, not a refutation of the power-law form.

A serviceable, frequently-updated overview that states the power-law form, lists the Kaplan and Chinchilla exponents side by side, and explains the C ≈ 6ND estimate. Useful for seeing the two papers reconciled in one place; check its citations rather than trusting figures blind.

expansion: Deeper treatment deliberately omitted from the prose, to be expanded strictly from the cited sources: (1) the exact Kaplan exponents and crossover constants with their fitted ranges and the joint loss surface L(N,D) including the finite-size and finite-data correction terms — Kaplan §§3-4; (2) the derivation of C ≈ 6ND from forward/backward FLOP counts — Kaplan appendix; (3) the compute-optimal frontier N_opt(C), D_opt(C) and the precise sense in which early models were under-trained — contrast Kaplan §6 against Hoffmann §3, including why the two analyses disagreed (learning-rate schedule treatment); (4) the three independent estimation methods in Chinchilla and their agreement. Cite each claim to its source section; introduce no numbers absent from the bibliography.
